To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) The process of risk assessment and risk management is fundamentally acceptable to U.S. courts; 2) QRA is an orderly procedure or methodology that is used to resolve cancer risk disputes; 3) QRA is not an unbiased process; 4) QRA is conservative; 5) QRA is dependent on a large number of uncertain assumptions; 6) QRA can be improved by substituting facts for assumptions
the process of risk assessment has not been improved in a meaningful way in the past 10 years.

the courts are willing to sustain regulatory decisions about risks if the technical methodologies used are in good standing, if the administrative procedures comply with the Administrative Procedure Act, and if the regulatory agencies are not acting in a capricious or risk-adverse manner.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following issues. First, the extent to which QRA is used in regulatory agencies
the development and application of a new approach to the quantitative estimation of cancer risk.
the process by which cancer risks are estimated.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

QRA is a process that can provide useful information for decision making but that it is not an exact science and therefore must always be considered in the light of the assumptions and uncertainties inherent in its application.
the process of risk assessment has been and will continue to be a dynamic process.
the process of establishing cancer risk tolerances is a very complex one that is subject to the influence of a large number of factors, some of which are not easily controlled.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the process of making risk estimates is fundamentally acceptable to regulatory agencies but the estimates are often criticized by the public as being too high.

the public is generally unaware that the process of risk estimation is fraught with assumptions, that risk estimation is a process that has been developed to resolve disputes, and that the process can be improved by substituting facts for assumptions.
the current system of risk assessment is not working well.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the QRA process is not broken. It is working as it was intended.
QRA is an imperfect process but that its imperfections are being recognized by the scientific and regulatory communities.
the process by which carcinogens are regulated must be improved.
